lead: On the Second Sunday after Pentecost the readings show what the Spirit does with those whom God calls. The evening Gospel (Luke 6:12–23) tells how Jesus spent the night in prayer and then chose the Twelve, and how he proclaimed the Beatitudes: “Blessed are you who are poor, for yours is the kingdom of God.” In 2 Samuel 5:1–10 the tribes come to David at Hebron and recall the Lord's word to him: “It is you who shall be shepherd of my people Israel.” In Baruch 1:2–8 the exiles in Babylon weep, fast and pray, and send gifts to Jerusalem. In Daniel 6:25–28, after Daniel has come safely out of the lions' den, King Darius confesses the God of Daniel, “the living God”, whose kingdom shall never be destroyed. In Acts 2:14–21 Peter explains Pentecost with the words of Joel: “I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh.”

We study three readings more closely. Leviticus gives the great command, “You shall be holy, for I the Lord your God am holy”, and shows that holiness reaches from the family table to the altar. Paul tells the Romans that there is no condemnation for those in Christ Jesus, because the Spirit of the one who raised Jesus now dwells in them. In Matthew, Jesus ends his sending of the Twelve with the cost and the reward of discipleship: whoever loses his life for his sake will find it, and even a cup of cold water given to a disciple will not lose its reward. The key words are holy, Spirit and welcome.

r.h: You shall be holy, for I am holy
set: Scholars call chapters 17–26 of Leviticus the Holiness Code, because of the refrain that runs through them: be holy, for I the Lord am holy. Leviticus took its final form, many scholars think, among the priests of Jerusalem, drawing on older laws. In the book itself these words are given by God to Moses at Sinai, for the whole people.

Chapter 19 is a remarkable mixture. Worship and daily life sit side by side: honour for parents, the sabbath, the ban on idols, the rules for sacrifice, care for the poor at harvest, honest weights, respect for the deaf and the blind, and at its centre the commandment “you shall love your neighbor as yourself” (19:18), which Jesus calls the second great commandment (Mark 12:31). For Leviticus, holiness is not one department of life. It is the whole of it.
str: vv. 1–2: the command to the whole congregation: be holy, because God is holy.
v. 3: reverence for mother and father; keeping the sabbath.
v. 4: no idols, no cast images.
vv. 5–8: the sacrifice of well-being: eaten on the first or second day, burned on the third.
¶ Verses 3 and 4 end with the signature “I am the Lord your God”, and verse 2 with “I the Lord your God am holy”.
kw: The root idea is “set apart”, belonging to God. Only God is holy in himself. Israel becomes holy by belonging to him and living in a way that shows it.
The Hebrew verb is the one used for the fear of God. Respect for parents is almost a religious duty. Unusually, the mother is named first, unlike the commandment in Exodus 20:12.

Also called the peace offering. Part of it was burned on the altar, and the rest was eaten by the worshippers in a sacred meal. It was the sacrifice of communion: God and his people sharing one table.
vv: You shall be holy, for I the Lord your God am holy.
Holiness is not first a moral achievement. It is a share in what God is. St Peter quotes this verse to the Christians of Asia Minor: “be holy yourselves in all your conduct” (1 Peter 1:15–16).
You shall each revere your mother and father, and you shall keep my sabbaths:
The first concrete sign of holiness is the home. The family and the day of rest are where reverence for God is first learned.
When you offer a sacrifice of well-being to the Lord, offer it in such a way that it is acceptable in your behalf.
The worshipper is responsible for how he worships. The gift must be offered in the way God has given, not in a way of our own invention.
It shall be eaten on the same day you offer it, or on the next day; and anything left over until the third day shall be consumed in fire.

The same rule is given in Leviticus 7:16–18. Many commentators think it kept the holy meal close to the offering and stopped sacred food from being treated as common. Verse 7 calls meat eaten on the third day piggûl, something spoiled and unclean.
ch: The Church hears in Leviticus 19:2 the universal call to holiness. The Second Vatican Council teaches that all the faithful, of whatever state or rank, are called to the fullness of Christian life and the perfection of charity (Lumen Gentium 40; CCC 2013). Christian readers have also seen in the sacrifice of well-being, offered to God and then shared at a holy meal, a distant sign of the Holy Qurbono, where the one sacrifice of Christ becomes the table of communion. The reverence that Leviticus demands for holy food teaches us how to approach the Body and Blood of the Lord.

r.h: No condemnation for those in Christ Jesus
set: Paul wrote Romans from Corinth around AD 57–58, to a church he had not yet visited. Chapter 7 ends with the cry of a person who knows God's law but cannot keep it: “Wretched man that I am! Who will rescue me from this body of death?” and the answer, “Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord!” (7:24–25). Chapter 8 unfolds that answer.

The word “Spirit” occurs about twenty times in chapter 8, more than in any other chapter of Paul. After the great feast of Pentecost, the Church reads this chapter to learn what life in the Spirit means day by day.
str: vv. 1–4: no condemnation: God has done in his Son what the law could not do.
vv. 5–8: two ways of setting the mind: on the flesh, which leads to death, or on the Spirit, which is life and peace.
vv. 9–11: the Spirit dwells in you, and the one who raised Jesus will give life to your mortal bodies.
kw: A legal word: the sentence passed on the guilty, with its penalty. Paul does not say there is no sin. He says the sentence has been lifted for those who are in Christ.
Not the body as such, and not sexuality only. In Paul it means human nature closed in on itself, relying on its own strength apart from God. The body itself is promised resurrection in verse 11.
The direction of the whole person: what we think about, desire and pursue. Life according to the Spirit is a matter of where the mind and heart are turned.
vv: There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.
“Now” is decisive. Something has changed in history, through the cross and resurrection, and in the believer, through Baptism.
For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has set you free from the law of sin and of death.
The “you” is singular in the best manuscripts; some read “me”. The POC keeps the singular “you”. Paul speaks to each believer personally.
by sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, and to deal with sin, he condemned sin in the flesh,

“To deal with sin” renders the Greek peri hamartias, the phrase the Greek Old Testament uses for the sin offering in Leviticus. The NRSV notes the other possible rendering, “as a sin offering”. Christ is the true offering that the old sacrifices pointed to.
If the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Christ from the dead will give life to your mortal bodies also through his Spirit that dwells in you.
The whole Trinity is in this verse: the Father who raises, the Son who was raised, the Spirit who dwells in us. The hope is not only for the soul but for the body.
ch: The Council of Trent took up verse 1 to teach that in those who are reborn in Baptism God hates nothing, and that there is no condemnation for those truly buried with Christ, even though an inclination to sin, called concupiscence, remains in them for the struggle (Decree on Original Sin, 5; see CCC 1264). The Catechism quotes verse 11 when it teaches the resurrection of the body: God will give life to our mortal bodies through his Spirit who dwells in us (CCC 989). Pentecost is therefore not only a feast of the past. The same Spirit lives in every baptized person.

set: Matthew arranges the teaching of Jesus in five great discourses. Chapter 10 is the second, the missionary discourse. Jesus names the Twelve (10:1–4), sends them first to “the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (10:6), and warns them of persecution, of division even within families, and of the cost of following him (10:16–37). Our verses close the discourse; the next verse says, “Now when Jesus had finished instructing his twelve disciples…” (11:1).

The passage moves from the cost of discipleship to the reward of those who receive disciples. Behind verse 40 stands a principle well known in Judaism and later written down in the Mishnah: one who is sent is like the one who sends him.
str: v. 40: to welcome the disciple is to welcome Christ, and the Father.
vv. 41–42: rewards: for welcoming a prophet, a righteous person, or one of the little ones.
kw: The Greek word can mean life, soul or self. The one who clings to his own life as a possession loses it; the one who spends it for Christ receives it back, now and in eternity.
The word for receiving a guest. It occurs four times in verse 40 alone. The mission of the Twelve depends on homes that open their doors.
Here the disciples themselves, the humble and unimportant messengers of Christ (compare 18:6). The smallest kindness to them is counted as done to him.
vv: and whoever does not take up the cross and follow me is not worthy of me.
This is the first time Matthew's Gospel mentions the cross. The disciples do not yet know how Jesus will die; Matthew's readers do.
Those who find their life will lose it, and those who lose their life for my sake will find it.
“For my sake” is the key. Jesus does not ask for loss for its own sake but for love of him. This saying is found in all four Gospels in some form (Mark 8:35; Luke 9:24; John 12:25).
Whoever welcomes you welcomes me, and whoever welcomes me welcomes the one who sent me.
A chain of sending: the Father sends the Son, the Son sends the apostles. To welcome the messenger is to welcome God himself.
and whoever gives even a cup of cold water to one of these little ones in the name of a disciple

Cold water in a hot land is the simplest gift there is. St John Chrysostom, preaching on this verse, points out that it costs nothing, so that no one can excuse himself on grounds of poverty (Homilies on Matthew, in substance).
ch: The Catechism teaches that Jesus is the Father's emissary and that he sends his apostles as the Father sent him, so that whoever receives them receives him (CCC 858). It also teaches that Jesus calls his disciples to take up their cross and follow him, because he wants to associate with his redeeming sacrifice those who are its first beneficiaries (CCC 618). These verses explain why the Church has always honoured those who welcome her missionaries and pastors: the family that houses a priest, the parish that supports a seminarian, the parents who give a son or daughter to God, all share in the reward of the one they welcome.

qa: If there is “no condemnation” for those in Christ, can a baptized Christian still be lost?

Paul's promise is for those who remain “in Christ”. In the same chapter he warns: “if you live according to the flesh, you will die” (8:13). The Church teaches that grave sin freely chosen can destroy charity and the life of grace in the soul (CCC 1861), and that Christ gave the sacrament of Reconciliation for those who fall after Baptism (CCC 1446). Our assurance is hope, not presumption: we trust in God's faithfulness and keep close to him (CCC 2005).
Why does Leviticus put a rule about leftover sacrificial meat next to “You shall be holy”?

Because for Leviticus holiness touches everything: the home, the sabbath, the altar and the table. The rule teaches that what is given to God is not to be handled carelessly. Christians apply the same lesson to the Holy Qurbono, approaching the Holy Mysteries with faith, reverence and a prepared heart.
Does “losing one's life” mean that Christians should look for suffering or death?

No. Jesus asks us to give our lives for his sake, not to seek pain for its own sake. The early Church honoured the martyrs but did not praise those who rushed to give themselves up; the account of St Polycarp's death says so plainly (Martyrdom of Polycarp 4). For most Christians, losing one's life for Christ means the daily gift of self: in a family, in service, in a vocation faithfully lived.
rite: Our Church keeps this Second Sunday after Pentecost as Vocations Day. In the West Syriac tradition the Sundays after Pentecost unfold the life of the Church that the Spirit has gathered, and today's readings fit the day closely: Jesus prays all night before he chooses the Twelve; David is called to be shepherd of God's people; the Spirit is poured out on sons and daughters, young and old; Titus, in yesterday's Epistle, is told to appoint elders in every town. Every vocation, to the priesthood, to religious life, to marriage and to mission, begins with God's call and is carried by the prayer of the Church. Jesus himself told us what to do: “ask the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into his harvest” (Matthew 9:38). Today every family is invited to pray for vocations by name, and to welcome those who answer, as the Gospel says, with at least a cup of cold water.
study: Leviticus says holiness begins with reverence for mother and father and with the sabbath. What would make my home and my Sunday more holy?
Paul says there is no condemnation for those in Christ Jesus. Is there an old guilt I still carry that I need to bring to the sacrament of Reconciliation and then leave behind?
Whom has the Lord sent to me, and how have I welcomed them: priests, religious, catechists, or simply people in need?
On this Vocations Day, whom can I encourage by name to listen to God's call, and how can our family support a vocation in our parish?
